Response to Show Cause Order 
 
Dear Secretary Reese: 
 
 
Pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”),1 Part 35 of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission’s (the “Commission”) regulations and Rules 209 and 213 of the 
Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,2 Trans Bay Cable LLC (“Trans Bay”) 
respectfully submits this response to the Commission’s Show Cause Order issued pursuant to 
section 206 of the FPA on June 18, 2026, in Docket No. EL26-71-000 directing the California 
Independent System Operator Corporation (“CAISO”) and Participating Transmission Owners 
(“PTOs”) in CAISO to show cause why their tariffs are just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory or preferential, or in the alternative to explain the necessary changes to remedy 
the Commission’s identified concerns.3  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission also 
encouraged a response in the form of a section 205 filing proposing tariff revisions remedying 
the concerns identified in the Show Cause Order.4  
 
In the instant filing, Trans Bay proposes revisions to its Transmission Owner Tariff 
(“Trans Bay Tariff”)5 and supporting explanations in response to the Show Cause Order to 
remedy the concerns identified therein.  Trans Bay’s proposed tariff revisions are just and 
reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and resolve the Commission’s 
applicable preliminary findings in the Show Cause Order.  Trans Bay also explains how certain

Further, Trans Bay respectfully requests a 30-day comment period on this filing.  Trans

effective February 16, 2027. The requested dates align with those requested by CAISO.  
I. 
BACKGROUND  
A. 
Trans Bay 
Trans Bay is a Non-LSE PTO in the CAISO region. Trans Bay is a public utility and 
subsidiary of NextEra Energy Transmission, LLC, that owns and operates a 53-mile, 
approximately 400 MW high-voltage direct current (“HVDC”) submarine transmission line 
buried at various depths beneath the San Francisco Bay, with AC/DC converter stations at each 
end (the “Trans Bay Cable”). The Trans Bay Cable provides direct electric transmission between 
the Pacific Gas & Electric Company (“PG&E”) Pittsburg Substation, located at a site adjacent to 
the City of Pittsburg, California, and PG&E’s Potrero Substation, located within the City of San 
Francisco. The Trans Bay Cable commenced commercial operation on November 23, 2010, and 
was simultaneously turned over to the operational control of the California Independent System 
Operator Corporation (“CAISO”). 
 
 
Trans Bay’s FPA-jurisdictional facilities consist of the Trans Bay Cable, as well as its 
CAISO Transmission Owner Tariff, rate schedules, and contracts on file with the Commission 
and related books and records. Trans Bay does not own or operate any generation or distribution 
facilities, nor does it engage in the sale or brokering of energy or ancillary services. Trans Bay 
recovers its transmission revenue requirement (“TRR”) through a Commission-approved stated 
rate under the Trans Bay Tariff, which is invoiced and collected through the CAISO Access 
Charge rates under Section 26 of the CAISO Open Access Transmission Tariff (“CAISO Tariff”).  
As a Non-LSE PTO under the CAISO Tariff and Transmission Control Agreement,7 Trans Bay 
serves no retail load.8 
B. 
Show Cause Order 
 
On June 18, 2026, the Commission initiated a show cause proceeding against CAISO and 
the PTOs pursuant to section 206 of the FPA.  The Show Cause Order directed CAISO and the 
PTOs to explain why the CAISO Tariff and the Transmission Owner Tariffs of the PTOs (“PTO 
Tariffs”) remain just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential without certain 
tariff provisions addressing:9

apply to Eligible Customers10 seeking transmission service on behalf of Large Loads; 
b) additional transparency concerning the network upgrade11 costs to provide transmission 
service to Eligible Customers on behalf of Large Loads; and a pro forma cost recovery 
agreement between CAISO, the relevant transmission owner, and the Eligible Customer 
taking transmission service on behalf of the Large Load to mitigate the risk of cost 
shifting among transmission customers, and a mechanism to ensure such payments are 
appropriately credited toward transmission owners’ TRRs consistent with the 
Commission’s cost-of-service regulations; 
c) the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to co-location arrangements; 
d) transmission services that reflect Eligible Customers taking transmission service on 
behalf of co-located loads, load with behind the meter generation, and flexible Large 
Loads that are willing and able to limit their use of the transmission system under certain 
conditions;12 and 
e) the rates, terms, and conditions of service applicable to interconnection customers serving 
electrically proximate Large Load or co-located load. 
Alternatively, respondents may explain what changes to their tariffs would remedy the identified 
concerns if the Commission were to determine that the tariffs have in fact become unjust and 
unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential and proceeds to establish a replacement 
tariff.13 
C. 
Motion for Abeyance 
 
On August 3, 2026, pursuant to Rule 212 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and 
Procedure, CAISO and the joint PTOs, which included Trans Bay, each filed motions to hold the 
above-referenced show cause proceeding in abeyance for 90 days, pending completion of 
CAISO’s stakeholder proceedings and development of the companies’ respective FPA section 
205 filings to address the Commission’s preliminary findings in the Show Cause Order

(“Abeyance Motions”).14  The Commission granted the Abeyance Motions and held this

II. 
TRANS BAY’S PROPOSED TRANSMISSION OWNER TARIFF REVISIONS 
 
The proposed Trans Bay Tariff revisions are just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory or preferential.  The proposed revisions establish an application process, study 
procedures, operational requirements, and creditworthiness and financial security requirements 
applicable to requests by Eligible Customers seeking to interconnect a Large Load to the Trans 
Bay transmission system.  The revisions are designed to consistently evaluate the reliability, 
operational, and planning impacts of proposed Large Loads, identify and allocate responsibility 
for any Direct Assignment Facilities, Reliability Upgrades, and other Network Upgrades, and 
mitigate the risk of cost shifting associated with the Interconnection and service of Large Loads.  
The proposed revisions provide transparency and certainty regarding the information, studies, 
agreements, and credit and financial security commitments required from Eligible Customers 
seeking transmission service on behalf of Large Loads.16  The proposed amendments to the Trans 
Bay Tariff fall into the following categories: 
(1) 
New and revised defined terms in Section 3 of its Trans Bay Tariff, including 
definitions of Large Load, Flexible Interim Load Interconnection (“FILI”) 
Service, Interconnection Facilities, Point of Interconnection, Network Upgrades, 
Site Control, Gross Load, Reliability Upgrade, Transmission Revenue 
Requirement; 
(2) 
Revisions to Section 5 of its Trans Bay Tariff to clarify Gross Load reporting 
associated with Large Load consistent with the CAISO Tariff; 
(3) 
Revisions to Sections 8.1 and 10.1 through 10.17 of its Trans Bay Tariff to 
establish an interconnection application process, readiness requirements, and 
study procedures specific to Large Load interconnections; 
(4) 
Revisions to Sections 8.1.5.1, 10.12, 10.17, and 16.12 of its Trans Bay Tariff to 
establish operational and reliability requirements for Large Loads; 
(5) 
Additions to Section 10.18 of the Trans Bay Tariff to establish rates, terms, and 
conditions of service applicable to co-located Large Load and FILI Service;

Completed Interconnection Application before February 16, 2027. 
Trans Bay’s proposed revisions are tailored to its status as a Non-LSE PTO, are 
coordinated with and consistent with proposed CAISO Tariff revisions and satisfy the Show 
Cause Order requirements applicable to a Non-LSE PTO.  Trans Bay has also incorporated 
certain conforming and ministerial revisions, such as correcting punctuation and applying 
consistent usage of terms.  Accordingly, Trans Bay respectfully submits that the proposed tariff 
revisions are just and reasonable, not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and should be 
accepted by the Commission under section 205 of the FPA, effective as requested.  Trans Bay 
further requests that the Commission terminate the show cause proceeding with respect to Trans 
Bay upon acceptance of the proposed tariff revisions. 
A. 
Large Load Interconnection Process 
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary finding that the CAISO 
Tariff and PTO Tariffs appear to be unjust and unreasonable because they lack clear and 
consistent provisions with respect to the application and study process for Eligible Customers 
seeking transmission and interconnection service on behalf of Large Loads.17  The Trans Bay 
Tariff establishes, in Sections 8.1 and 10, a defined and time-limited interconnection process for 
Large Loads with specific application, readiness, study, and operational requirements, and it 
clarifies how a Large Load interconnected to Trans Bay’s facilities obtains transmission service 
over the CAISO Controlled Grid.  Elements of this proposal include the following tariff 
improvements for the integration of Large Loads. 
1. 
Definition of Large Load   
Commission Concerns:  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary 
finding that the CAISO Tariff and PTO Tariffs appear to be unjust and unreasonable because they 
lack a definition of Large Load sufficient to capture loads that present the unique challenges 
described in the Show Cause Order.18 
Trans Bay Solution:  In response to the Commission’s finding, Trans Bay proposes to 
define a Large Load as “[a]n End-User located at a single site behind one or more Points of 
 
17  Show Cause Order at PP 38, 49, 58.  Citations herein to the “Trans Bay Tariff” refer to the revised Trans Bay 
TO Tariff included as Appendices A and B to this filing.  Citations to the “CAISO Proposed Tariff” refer to the tariff 
revisions CAISO is submitting contemporaneously in response to the Show Cause Order. 
18  Show Cause Order at PP 56, 57.

6 
Interconnection to the CAISO Controlled Grid, and that has a peak load of 50 MW or greater.”19 
This definition is identical to the definition CAISO proposes to add to Appendix A of the CAISO 
Tariff, and adopts the 50 MW threshold the Commission identified as reasonable.20  Trans Bay 
has also adopted CAISO’s approach of not excluding co-located loads from the definition of 
Large Load to ensure alignment between the two tariffs. 
2. 
Application and Study Procedures 
Commission Concerns:  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary 
finding that the CAISO Tariff and PTO Tariffs appear to be unjust and unreasonable because they 
lack clear and consistent provisions addressing the application process and study procedures for 
Eligible Customers to request transmission service on behalf of Large Loads.21  The Commission 
indicated that such processes should clarify that applications be accepted on a rolling basis; 
require a non-refundable application fee as well as staged readiness requirements; and specify 
the information and data requirements to be submitted with an application.22 
Trans Bay Solution:  The proposed tariff revisions leverage Trans Bay’s existing 
application and study processes while identifying the additional procedures applicable to Large 
Loads due to their unique operational requirements and reliability impacts on the transmission 
system.  Trans Bay submits that this approach promotes transparency and administrative 
efficiency by providing a single, integrated framework for Large Load interconnection requests 
under the Trans Bay Tariff.  This is responsive to the Show Cause Order’s concern regarding the 
lack of specificity for Large Loads and their unique operational characteristics and requirements. 
Trans Bay’s proposed tariff revisions establish the applicable provisions for Eligible 
Customers requesting service on behalf of Large Loads (as defined in the Trans Bay Tariff).  
First, revised Section 8.1 explicitly extends Trans Bay’s obligation to interconnect to entities 
eligible to request interconnection to pursuant to FPA section 210(a) and Eligible Customers, 
including Large Loads owned or served by a third party.  Because Trans Bay is a Non-LSE PTO 
with no retail customers, a Large Load connecting directly to Trans Bay’s facilities may not 
qualify as an “Eligible Customer” in certain instances.  Trans Bay therefore proposes, in new 
Section 10.2, a voluntary offer of unbundled retail transmission service, where consistent with 
state law, so that Large Loads can request Interconnection and be studied under the Trans Bay 
Tariff as the Show Cause Order contemplates.23 Second, revised Section 10.1 requires that a 
Large Load Interconnection be requested pursuant to Section 10 of the Trans Bay Tariff and

Tariff, applications are accepted on a rolling basis, and revised Section 10.4 requires Trans Bay

Consistent with the Commission’s concern that the tariffs specify which entity is 
responsible for the study, Trans Bay is proposing revisions to Sections 10.1 and 10.4 to clarify 
that the Eligible Customer is the entity that requests Interconnection on behalf of a Large Load.25 
Trans Bay, as the interconnecting PTO, will perform the System Impact Study and Facilities 
Study for the Eligible Customer taking transmission service on behalf of a Large Load pursuant 
to Section 10.26  As part of its study obligations, Trans Bay will apprise CAISO of Large Load 
interconnections through its inputs to the Base Case, Interconnection Studies, and the 
Transmission Planning Process.27  Prior to energization of any Large Load, Trans Bay must 
provide CAISO the information required by Section 25.7.1 of the CAISO Tariff, and the Eligible 
Customer must provide that information to Trans Bay and notify Trans Bay of any material 
changes within 10 Business Days.28  
Furthermore, Trans Bay proposes new Section 10.5.1 to clarify additional application 
requirements for Large Load interconnections.  Specifically, an Eligible Customer seeking to 
interconnect a Large Load must submit: (i) the Large Load’s ramp schedule, identifying load 
additions over time and maximum planned load; (ii) a site plan; (iii) documentation of the local, 
state, and federal permits and regulatory approvals necessary to develop the Large Load; (iv) 
documentation demonstrating Site Control; (v) a single-line electrical diagram; (vi) information 
on any other Interconnection requests made on behalf of the same Large Load or its affiliates; 
(vii) whether the Large Load intends to request Partial Interim Service or FILI Service; and (viii) 
for a Large Load co-located with a Generating Facility, information sufficient for Trans Bay to 
ensure compliance with Sections 25.1.1, 25.7.5, and 25.7.6 of the CAISO Tariff.  Because 
Section 10.3 requires every Interconnection Application to be copied to CAISO, Section 
10.5.1(vi) requires disclosure of other pending requests on behalf of the same Large Load to 
CAISO, as the Commission contemplated.29  Trans Bay and CAISO, as applicable, must 
determine whether an application is complete within ten (10) Business Days under Section 10.6. 
An applicant must pay a $5,000 nonrefundable Large Load Interconnection Application 
fee.30  At the time of application, they must provide site plans, demonstration of Site Control

requirements will ensure that interconnection applications are real, concrete, and nonspeculative.  
Furthermore, Trans Bay proposes that, at the Large Load System Impact Study phase, the 
Eligible Customer must provide a refundable study deposit of: (a) $35,000 plus $1,000 per MW 
for Interconnection Requests less than 80 MW; (b) $150,000 for Interconnection Requests 
greater than or equal to 80 MW but less than 200 MW; or (c) $250,000 for Interconnection 
Requests greater than 200 MW.32 The refundable study deposit amounts are consistent with those 
required in CAISO’s generator interconnection process.  At the Facilities Study phase, the 
Eligible Customer must pay the estimated cost of the Facilities Study, and, before energization, 
amongst other requirements, it must execute the Interconnection Agreement and pro forma Cost 
Recovery Agreement, and post all required financial security (Sections 10.17.2, 8.1.5.1(viii), and 
13.2.1).  These readiness requirements thus escalate at distinct phases throughout the study 
process, consistent with the Show Cause Order directives.33  An applicant that withdraws from 
the process at any phase must reimburse Trans Bay for all costs reasonably incurred and may be 
responsible for the cost of restudying later-queued applicants.  
For a Large Load Interconnection, the System Impact Study must evaluate the Large 
Load’s operational characteristics, including its ramp schedule, its performance during system 
disturbances, and any ability to limit its withdrawals from the CAISO Controlled Grid, consistent 
with Section 25.7.1 of the CAISO Tariff.  The PTO will evaluate impacts to the transmission 
system using power flow and short circuit analyses, and any other analyses that may be 
appropriate including Electromagnetic Transient studies where warranted.  The completed 
System Impact Study will include a non-binding, good-faith estimate of the cost of Direct 
Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades needed to accommodate the request and the time 
required to construct them, which the Facilities Study then refines.  Trans Bay may request 
additional information, data, or models reasonably needed for the study, including models 
suitable for Electromagnetic Transient studies.  The request then proceeds through Trans Bay’s 
existing Facilities Study procedures, which refine the facilities design and the cost and schedule 
estimates for incorporation into the Interconnection Agreement. 
3. 
Operational and Reliability Requirements  
Commission Concerns:  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary 
finding that the CAISO Tariff and PTO Tariffs appear to be unjust and unreasonable because they 
lack appropriate provisions regarding the ongoing operational requirements that will apply to 
transmission customers serving Large Loads.34  The Commission further highlighted the lack of 
detail on data available to CAISO regarding interconnected Large Loads for monitoring and 
reliability purposes, the lack of language enabling CAISO to remotely disconnect Large Loads

via installed equipment, the absence of specified ramp rate, ride-through, and control 
technologies or protection systems required.35  
Trans Bay Solution:  It is Trans Bay’s understanding that CAISO is proposing changes 
to Section 25.7.1 of the CAISO Tariff to provide substantial additional clarity regarding ongoing 
operational requirements for Eligible Customers serving Large Loads, including Frequency Ride-
Through, Voltage Ride-Through, Post-Fault Active Power Recovery, and Ramp-Rate Limitation 
requirements.  Accordingly, Trans Bay’s proposed Section 10.17 specifies that any Large Load 
Interconnection Agreement will require compliance with Section 25.7.1 of the CAISO Tariff, and 
proposed Section 10.3 requires Trans Bay to provide the information required by Section 25.7.1 
to CAISO prior to energization of the Large Load.  This approach will ensure that Large Load 
operational requirements remain current with CAISO standards and provide transparency and 
regularity of operational standards that will support reliable operation of the overall grid.   
Trans Bay also proposes a series of additional operational requirements mirroring CAISO 
Tariff measures, specifically:  
 Following proposed CAISO Tariff Section 25.7.4 by requiring the Eligible 
Customer, Large Load, Scheduling Coordinator, and Trans Bay to comply with 
any CAISO, Regional Entity, or Reliability Coordinator data request after a 
disturbance or other reliability event involving a Large Load (Section 16.12); 
 Ensuring visibility into Large Load operations by extending proposed CAISO 
Tariff Section 25.7.3 requirements for the Scheduling Coordinator for each Large 
Load to provide daily and hourly forecasts, material real-time deviations, outage 
information, and real-time telemetry (Sections 8.1.5.1(iii) and 10.17); and 
 Following proposed CAISO Tariff Sections 25.7.1.1, 25.7.1.2, 25.7.1.3, and 
25.7.1.4, by requiring Large Load to meet all frequency ride-through 
requirements, voltage ride through requirements, post-fault active power recovery 
requirements, and ramp rate limitations established therein (Section 8.1.5.1(x)). 
Finally, Trans Bay proposes requirements for installation and maintenance of the 
equipment required to disconnect or otherwise isolate the Large Load (Sections 8.1.5.1(vi) and 
10.17), with those costs directly assigned to the applicant to avoid cost shifting to transmission 
customers (Section 8.1.2). 
4. 
Alternative Transmission Technologies   
Commission Concerns:  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary 
finding that the CAISO Tariff and PTO Tariffs appear to be unjust and unreasonable because they 
lack clear and consistent provisions requiring the evaluation of alternative transmission 
technologies as potential solutions to an Eligible Customer’s request for service on behalf of a 
Large Load,36 or requiring an explanation to the Eligible Customer why alternative transmission 
 
35  Id. at P 63. 
36  Id. at P 60.

10 
technologies are not feasible or would not result in lower costs or a faster timeline 
accommodating the request.37  
Trans Bay Solution:  The proposed revisions to Section 10.12.1 commit Trans Bay to 
considering alternative transmission technologies in the System Impact Study for every Large 
Load Interconnection Application, without the need for a request from the Eligible Customer.  If 
Trans Bay selects traditional Network Upgrades instead, it must demonstrate why alternative 
transmission technologies are not feasible or would not result in lower costs or a faster timeline 
for accommodating the request.38  This provision is consistent with the proposed revision to 
CAISO Tariff Section 24.1, which extends CAISO’s consideration of alternative transmission 
technologies to Large Loads and contemplates the inclusion of similar language in the PTO 
Tariffs. 
5. 
Study Process Timeline 
Commission Concerns:  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary 
finding that the study processes could culminate in a report to the Eligible Customer describing 
the Network Upgrades necessary to accommodate the service request as well as a non-binding 
good-faith estimate of the cost and the time to construct such facilities, which should take no 
more than 60-90 calendar days to complete.39  
Trans Bay Solution:  Trans Bay proposes the adoption of revised Section 10.12 and 
10.12.1 to its tariff requiring that a System Impact Study for a Large Load provide a non-binding, 
good-faith estimate of the cost of Direct Assignment Facilities and Network Upgrades needed to 
accommodate the request and a similar good-faith time estimate required to construct them.  
Following the System Impact Study, pursuant to Section 10.16 the Facilities Study will refine 
those estimates leading into the Interconnection Agreement process.40  The report will be 
available following the System Impact Study, consistent with the Show Cause Order directive.  
Trans Bay also recognizes the need for timely progression of required studies.  
Accordingly, the proposed Trans Bay Tariff revisions shorten the timeline for interconnection 
studies at each step of the process to the maximum extent achievable (Sections 10.8 - 10.12).  
Under the proposed Large Load study procedures, Trans Bay must notify the applicant whether a 
System Impact Study is required within ten (10) Business Days of the Completed Application 
Date and must tender a System Impact Study Agreement within ten (10) Business Days of 
receipt of the Completed Interconnection Application.  The applicant must execute that 
agreement within ten (10) Business Days and, for a Large Load Interconnection, remit a study 
deposit together with financial security drawable to cover System Impact Study costs and, if 
necessary, Facilities Study costs.  Trans Bay must complete the System Impact Study no later 
than ninety (90) Calendar Days after the Completed Application Date.  This 90-day timeline runs 
from the Completed Application Date, not from execution of the System Impact Study

Agreement, and therefore includes the time for the System Impact Study Agreement and deposit 
steps.  The result of this proposed schedule is the initiation and completion of a System Impact 
Study within the 60-90 calendar day range that the Commission identified as reasonable.  
 
This proposed structure is consistent with the study process the Commission accepted for 
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”) High Impact Large Loads (“HILL”).  For that process, 
SPP must complete its HILL Delivery Point Study and issue a study report within 90 calendar 
days after receiving the executed study agreement, study data, and deposit.41  That study uses 
power flow and short circuit analyses; SPP then performs an Electromagnetic Transient study 
only when those analyses identify system weaknesses caused by the Large Load, similar to Trans 
Bay’s Large Load System Impact Study process.42  The HILL Delivery Point Study works “in 
conjunction with” SPP’s existing load connection study requirements.43  It is followed, as 
needed, by a supplemental load connection study performed by the host transmission owner and 
by SPP’s existing processes for obtaining long-term transmission service.  SPP’s tariff does not 
subject those later steps to the 90-day deadline,44 but the Commission found this process just and 
reasonable.45  Trans Bay’s approach follows the same structure.  A time-certain System Impact 
Study culminates in a report within 90 days, and that report gives the Eligible Customer the 
information the Show Cause Order requires. 
B. 
Co-Located Load  
Commission Concerns:  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary 
finding that the CAISO Tariff appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it lacks sufficiently 
clear and consistent tariff provisions addressing the rates, terms, and conditions that apply to co-
location arrangements.46  
Trans Bay Solution:  As acknowledged by the Commission in its Show Cause Order and 
further addressed in Part III below, Trans Bay has a limited role in addressing co-location of 
generation with Large Load.  The interconnection of wholesale generation to the CAISO 
Controlled Grid is governed by the CAISO Tariff, including the Resource Interconnection 
Standards in Appendix KK.  Trans Bay’s role is to process and study the Interconnection of a 
Large Load and to coordinate with CAISO so that the generating facility and the Large Load are 
studied, interconnected, and operated together.  As revised, the Trans Bay Tariff and CAISO 
Tariff jointly allocate those responsibilities.

Cost Shifting and Cost Recovery Agreements 
Commission Concerns:  In the Show Cause Order, the Commission made a preliminary 
finding that the CAISO Tariff and PTO Tariffs appear to be unjust and unreasonable because they 
lack adequate mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers.54  
The Show Cause Order directed the PTOs to address: (i) assignment of the Network Upgrade 
costs and their associated costs, that are needed to provide transmission service to Eligible 
Customers serving Large Loads; (ii) the need for a pro forma cost recovery agreement to 
mitigate the risk of cost shifting; and (iii) a mechanism to ensure that any payments attributable 
to the Large Load are appropriately credited toward the PTO’s TRR and documented in the 
annual informational filing for formula rates.55  The Commission also indicated a response 
should clarify how the minimum contribution and financial security required by an Eligible 
Customer serving a Large Load is calculated, i.e., whether by a per-MW figure or another 
methodology.56 
Trans Bay Solution:  Through Section 10.17.2, Trans Bay will utilize a Cost Recovery 
Agreement in the form of Attachment A to the Trans Bay Tariff to address assignment of costs 
associated with the construction and operation of any Network Upgrades resulting from the 
Interconnection of the Large Load.  The Cost Recovery Agreement will be between Trans Bay 
and the Eligible Customer, and CAISO may join at its election.57  The Cost Recovery Agreement 
requires the Eligible Customer to pay 100% of the actual costs of the Large Load Network 
Upgrades through the Total Required Revenue Commitment.  The Total Required Revenue 
Commitment establishes both the obligation to pay actual costs and the obligation to maintain 
financial security for the Eligible Customer.  If the Eligible Customer does not provide sufficient 
service revenue attributable to the Large Load to Trans Bay through CAISO’s Access Charges to 
cover the Eligible Customer’s Annual Required Revenue Commitment, the Eligible Customer 
must provide Cost Recovery Payments to fill the gap in cost recovery.  Cost Recovery

security shall be decreased as the Eligible Customer pays the Total Required Revenue 
Commitment over time.  Trans Bay may draw upon the required financial security in the event of 
non-payment, termination, cancellation, or withdrawal to ensure that the Large Load is 
responsible for costs incurred to provide transmission service, including the cost of network 
upgrades and to prevent cost shifting to other customers.  
Trans Bay has not proposed to allow an Eligible Customer to satisfy the financial security 
required under the Cost Recovery Agreement with credit support posted under a retail agreement.  
The Commission’s preliminary finding that an Eligible Customer “may include” such security 
permits this approach but does not require it.59  The approach does not fit a Non-LSE PTO.  
Trans Bay has no retail customers and is not party to any retail service agreement.  Any retail 
security would be held by a third-party load-serving entity, would secure that entity’s retail 
obligations, and be subject to that entity’s draw rights and priorities, none of which Trans Bay 
can control or enforce.  Such security therefore would not be sufficient to secure the Eligible 
Customer’s obligations under the Cost Recovery Agreement.  Accepting it would leave other 
transmission customers exposed to the cost-shifting risk the Order is intended to prevent.  The 
concern about duplicative credit requirements also does not arise here.  The security required 
under the Cost Recovery Agreement secures a separate, Commission-jurisdictional payment 
obligation owed to Trans Bay, not the retail obligation owed to the load-serving entity.  
Requiring a single form of security held directly by the transmission owner is also simpler to 
administer and applies uniformly.    
Trans Bay Tariff Section 10.17 requires the Interconnection Agreement itself to include 
cost responsibilities, financial security, and payment provisions for all engineering, equipment, 
construction, ownership, operation, and maintenance costs of any Direct Assignment Facilities, 
Reliability Upgrades, Interconnection Facilities, or Network Upgrades.  Section 8.1.2 requires 
the party requesting Interconnection to pay all such costs, and Trans Bay has specified that this 
includes Interconnection for Large Loads throughout the Trans Bay Tariff.   
Lastly, Trans Bay’s Section 13.2.1 requires Trans Bay to conduct reasonable credit review 
procedures and obtain financial security from the Eligible Customer.  The financial security may 
take the form of an unconditional and irrevocable letter of credit or an alternative form 
acceptable to Trans Bay and consistent with commercial practices under the Uniform 
Commercial Code, in the amount of the Total Required Revenue Commitment set forth in the 
Cost Recovery Agreement.60  Trans Bay’s Tariff conditions Large Load energization on posting

IV. 
RESPONSES TO THE COMMISSION’S REMAINING BRIEFING QUESTIONS 
The Show Cause Order requested responses to specific briefing questions.72  Consistent 
with the division of responsibilities between CAISO and the PTOs recognized by the 
Commission in the Show Cause Order, Trans Bay responds to those briefing questions applicable 
to it as a PTO and defers to CAISO on those questions directed to CAISO or that concern matters 
governed by the CAISO Tariff.  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission recognized that the framework under which 
CAISO provides transmission service is unique among the RTOs/ISOs and that certain 
responsibilities fall to the PTOs.  The Commission explained that the PTOs “have responsibility 
for wholesale load interconnection studies,” while CAISO “is responsible for access to and the 
provision of transmission service, including transmission and ancillary services, to all Eligible 
Customers, and the reliability of that transmission service.”73  The Commission further 
recognized that the PTOs may be primarily responsible for conducting the studies that evaluate 
whether a Large Load may be interconnected to the transmission system and whether Network 
Upgrades are necessary, that this role stems from how CAISO and the PTOs allocated rights and 
responsibilities in the governing documents establishing CAISO, and that the Commission does 
not seek to alter that allocation of rights and responsibilities.74  Consistent with that framework, 
the Commission directed the PTOs to respond to the extent the matters addressed herein 
implicate aspects of their respective tariffs.75 
Within this framework, Trans Bay’s role is to process and study requests to interconnect 
Eligible Customer Large Loads to its facilities under the Trans Bay Tariff, to construct any Direct 
Assignment Facilities and Reliability Upgrades required for those interconnections and recover 
their costs from the Eligible Customer, and to provide CAISO with the necessary information for 
its operations and its Transmission Planning Process.  Transmission service over the CAISO 
Controlled Grid, including Trans Bay’s facilities, is provided by CAISO under the CAISO Tariff.  
CAISO likewise administers the CAISO Markets and the generator interconnection procedures 
under the CAISO Tariff, and the California Public Utilities Commission has primary 
responsibility for resource adequacy within the CAISO footprint.76  Moreover, as a Non-LSE 
PTO, Trans Bay serves no retail load and does not forecast or plan for load growth within a retail 
service territory.
